title based on wikidata|qid=Q11649485}} from which one can overlook both the {{ill|Suzuka River|en|Suzuka River|qid=Q7651182|lt=Suzuka River}} flowing toward {{ill|Ise Bay|en|Ise Bay|qid=Q1368308|lt=Ise Bay}} and the {{ill|Tamura River|ja|田村川|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tamura River|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q17172424}} flowing from {{ill|Lake Biwa|en|Lake Biwa|qid=Q200239|lt=Lake Biwa}}. {{Sfn|阿部|2004|pages=88-93}}{{Sfn|桐村|2012|pages=117-121}}

The surrounding area is a sacred land blessed with abundant water. It is renowned as the site of the Suzuka Misogi, where the Saio ({{ill|Saiō|en|Saiō|qid=Q19841349|lt=Saio}}) en route to {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|en|Ise Shrine|qid=Q687168|lt=Ise Grand Shrine}} once stayed to perform misogi ({{ill|Misogi|en|Misogi|qid=Q1936265|lt=Misogi}}), and later became consecrated by shamanic practitioners ({{ill|Wu (shaman)|ja|巫覡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shamanic Practitioner|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 巫|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q3687892}}) performing purification rituals ({{ill|Harae|ja|祓え|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Purification Ritual|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 祓|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q3127244}}). 

Within the precincts stand the monument commemorating the origin of Suzuka-ryu naginatajutsu – {{ill|Suzuka-ryū‎|ja|鈴鹿流|lt=Suzuka-ryu Naginatajutsu Origin|lt_ja=鈴鹿流薙刀術発生之地|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Suzuka-ryu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11649496}} – and a monument honoring the filial piety of Bankichi.

== History ==
=== Founding ===
The exact founding date is unknown. Originally, the three mountains of Mikoyama ({{ill|Suzuka-dake|ja|鈴鹿嶽}}, {{ill|Takenamada-dake|ja|武名嶽}}, and {{ill|Takahata-dake|ja|高幡嶽}}) located on the eastern side of the Suzuka Pass were revered as a sacred mountain ({{ill|Sacred mountains|en|Sacred mountains|qid=Q1595289|lt=Sacred Mountain}}). On its central peak, {{ill|Seoritsu-hime|ja|瀬織津姫|lt=Seoritsu-hime}} was enshrined, while on the left and right peaks {{ill|Ibuki-do-nushi|ja|伊吹戸主}} and {{ill|Hayasasurahime|ja|速佐須良姫}} were respectively honored. However, a fire caused the transfer of the enshrinement to the old Suzuka Tondo Shrine. Subsequent repeated transfers due to frequent fires led to a unification of the shrine enshrining Yamato-hime – known as the Suzuka Shrine ({{ill|Suzuka Shrine|ja|鈴鹿社}}) – with the four deities, and later five additional deities including {{ill|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|en|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|qid=Q941979|lt=Sakanoue no Tamuramaro}} were added. In the 2nd year of the Einin Era ({{ill|Einin|en|Einin|qid=Q1327307|lt=Einin Era}} 2, 1294), the shrine was relocated to the area of Tatsukami Saka and became the guardian shrine of Sakasita-juku ({{ill|Sakashita-juku|en|Sakashita-juku|qid=Q3033376|lt=Sakasita-juku}}) enshrining Suzuka-hime. In the 40th year of the Meiji Era ({{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}} 40, 1907), the Tamura Shrine ({{ill|Tamura Shrine|ja|田村神社}}) near the Kagami Rock of Suzuka Pass was merged, forming the present structure.

=== General History ===
Due to its location on the border ({{ill|State border|ja|国境|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Provincial Border|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q12413618}}) between {{ill|Ise Province|en|Ise Province|qid=Q864166|lt=Ise Province}} and {{ill|Ōmi Province|en|Ōmi Province|qid=Q843882|lt=Ōmi Province}}, {{ill|Q104539506|ja|鈴鹿山|qid=Q104539506}} was a key transportation hub since ancient times. Consequently, numerous legends concerning demons ({{ill|Oni|ar|أوني|az|Oni (iblis)|bcl|Oni|be|Оні (міфалогія)|ca|Oni|cs|Oni (mytologie)|de|Oni|eo|Onio|es|Oni (folclore japonés)|eu|Oni|fa|اونی (فولکلور ژاپنی)|fi|Oni (Japani)|fr|Oni|hu|Oni|hy|Օնիներ (դևեր)|id|Oni|it|Oni (folclore)|ja|鬼|jv|Oni (cerita rakyat)|ka|ონი (დემონები)|ko|오니 (요괴)|mk|Они|ms|Oni|nl|Oni (mythisch wezen)|nn|Oni|no|Oni (folklore)|pl|Oni|pt|Oni|ro|Oni|ru|Они (демоны)|sh|Oni (folklor)|simple|Oni (folklore)|sq|Oni|sv|Oni|th|โอนิ|tr|Oni|uk|Оні|vi|Oni|xmf|ონი (დემონეფი)|zh|鬼 (日本)|zh_yue|鬼 (妖怪)|qid=Q730052|lt=Oni}}) and bandits ({{ill|Banditry|af|Struikrowery|ar|لصوصية|az|Banditizm|be|Бандытызм|bg|Бандитизъм|bh|डकइती|ca|Bandolerisme|cdo|Tū-pī|ce|ЖӀакки|cy|Banditiaeth|es|Bandidismo organizado|et|Banditism|fa|راهزنی|fr|Banditisme|gl|Bandidaxe|ha|Banditry|hi|डकैती|hy|Ավազակություն|id|Kebanditan|it|Banditismo|ja|盗賊|kk|Бандитизм|ko|도적|pt|Banditismo|ru|Бандитизм|tg|Бандитизм|tr|Eşkıyalık|uk|Бандитизм|uz|Jinoiy uyushma|vec|Banditismo|vi|Thổ phỉ|zh|土匪|qid=Q10968653|lt=Bandits}}) have been handed down regarding the Suzuka Pass. Toward the end of the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian Period}}, the name “{{ill|Suzuka Gozen|ja|鈴鹿御前|zh|鈴鹿御前|qid=Q11649495|lt=Standing Eboshi}}” appears in the {{ill|Hobutsushu|ja|宝物集|qid=Q5875266|lt=Treasury Collection}}, and local legends relate that although {{ill|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|en|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|qid=Q941979|lt=Sakanoue no Tamuramaro}} was ordered to subdue the Standing Eboshi, the two became husband and wife; after their deaths, the locals of the Suzuka Pass enshrined the Standing Eboshi as Suzuka Gomen and honored Tamuramaro in the Tamura Hall. {{Sfn|桐村|2012|pages=117-121}}

In the {{ill|Nara Picture Book|ja|奈良絵本}} ‘Suzuka’, the Standing Eboshi of Suzuka is described as the Gongen of Suzuka, serving as the guardian deity ({{ill|Guardian deities|ja|守護神|qid=Q131278957}}) of the {{ill|Tōkaidō (region)|ca|Tōkaidō|ckb|تۆکایدۆ|es|Tōkaidō (región)|fa|توکایدو|it|Tōkaidō (regione)|ja|東海道|ko|도카이도|lt|Tokaido (sritis)|min|Tokaido|pl|Tōkaidō (region)|pt|Tōkaidō (região)|ru|Токайдо|simple|Tōkaidō (region)|sr|Токаидо (регион)|tr|Tōkaidō|uk|Східноморський край|zh|東海道|zh_min_nan|Tôkaidô|zh_yue|東海道|qid=Q1196306|lt=Tōkaidō}}, protecting travelers in place of their own persons so that those journeying along the road would be spared misfortune. Furthermore, numerous small ritual vessels excavated in the vicinity of the Suzuka Pass suggest that travelers offered them in prayer for safe passage, indicating that the site functioned as a shrine festival remnant (and exhibiting characteristics of a Dosojin ({{ill|Dōsojin|de|Dōsojin|es|Dōsojin|fi|Dōsojin|fr|Dōsojin|hu|Dószodzsin|id|Dōsojin|it|Dōsojin|ja|道祖神|ko|도소진|mk|Сае но Ками|th|โดโซจิง|zh|道祖神|qid=Q269515|lt=Dosojin}}) type deity). {{Sfn|阿部|2004|pages=88-93}}

Much like the {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|bg|Кшитигарбха|bn|ক্ষিতিগর্ভ|bo|ས་ཡི་སྙིང་པོ།|ca|Ksitigarbha|cs|Kšitigarbha|de|Kshitigarbha|el|Τζίζο|eo|Kŝitigarbo|es|Ksitigarbha|fa|کشیتی‌گربه|fr|Kshitigarbha|hu|Dzsizó|id|Kṣitigarbha|it|Kṣitigarbha|ja|地蔵菩薩|ka|ქშიტიგარბჰა|km|ក្សិតិគភ៌|ko|지장보살|mk|Џизо Бозацу|nl|Ksitigarbha|pl|Ksitigarbha|pt|Dizang|ro|Ksitigarbha|ru|Кшитигарбха|simple|Kṣitigarbha|sv|Ksitigarbha|ta|இக்சிதிகர்பர்|th|พระกษิติครรภโพธิสัตว์|tr|Ksitigarbha|uk|Кшітіґарбга|vi|Địa Tạng|wuu|地藏菩萨|zh|地藏菩萨|zh_min_nan|Tē-chōng-phô͘-sat|zh_yue|地藏菩薩|qid=Q604687}} enshrined on {{ill|Mount Atago|en|Mount Atago|qid=Q2975204|lt=Atago Mountain}} in Kyoto, the Kagami Rock (also referred to as Kagamaseki) at the Suzuka Pass—regarded as an iwasaka ({{ill|Iwakura rock|en|Iwakura rock|qid=Q11587880|lt=Iwasaka}})—lies on the boundary between Kyoto ({{ill|Kyōto|ja|京都|lt=Kyoto|lt_ja=京|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q740246}}) and Tanba ({{ill|Tanba Province|en|Tanba Province|qid=Q954511|lt=Tanba}}). There, by enshrining General Tamura within the rock, he was revered as a “general Jizō” in tandem with Suzuka Gongen, evidencing an ancient faith in Saino no Kami ({{ill|Q115978710|ja|塞の神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saino no Kami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q115978710}}). This belief later evolved into the legend of Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, as recounted in otogi-zōshi such as ‘Suzuka no Sōshi’ and ‘Standing Eboshi’, as well as in the {{ill|Okujoruri|ja|奥浄瑠璃|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Okujōruri|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q109361758}} text ‘Tamura Sandai-ki’, which narrates the tale of General Tamura and Suzuka Gomen as a divine couple battling the demon god ({{ill|Ootakemaru|en|Ootakemaru|qid=Q30926182|lt=Demon God}}). {{Sfn|阿部|2004|pages=88-93}}

In the Shintō collection (‘{{ill|Shintōshū|en|Shintōshū|qid=Q2616931|lt=Shintō Shū}}’), it is recorded that “the parents of Kakuwa-dono were also taught the principles of Shintō, and became the Suzuka Daimyōjin of the Iga Province Sannomiya”; however, since the Iga Sannomiya is identified with {{ill|Hataki Shrine|ja|波多岐神社}}, this is suspected to be a misprint for the Ise Province Sannomiya. {{Refnest|group=注|『神道集』「児持山大明神の事」}}

During the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|qid=Q184963|lt=Edo Period}}, the published work ‘{{ill|Ise Grand Shrine Famous Places Illustrated|ja|伊勢参宮名所図会}}’ in its “Suzuka Mountain” section depicts, separated by the Kagami Rock of the Suzuka Pass, a bolded “Suzuka Shrine” on the Ise side and, on the Ōmi side, a Tamura Myōjin (a shrine distinct from {{ill|Tamura Shrine (Koka City)|ja|田村神社 (甲賀市)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tamura Shrine (Kōka)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11576975}}), with an accompanying explanation stating that Suzuka Shrine was also known by alternate names such as Katayama Shrine and the bolded “Prefectural Shrine”. {{Sfn|桐村|2012|pages=117-121}}

An inscribed stone pillar at the ruins of Tamura Shrine records that in the 40th year of the Meiji Era (1907) it was merged into Katayama Shrine; thus, the Tamura Shrine known as Tamura Myōjin during the Edo Period was incorporated into Katayama Shrine. {{Sfn|桐村|2012|pages=117-121}}

In the 11th year of the Heisei Era (1999), the main hall was burned down due to arson.

== Landmarks and Historic Sites ==
* Kagami Rock of Suzuka Mountain (Kagamaseki, Kagamihada)
* The ruins of Tamura Shrine (also known as Tamura Hory or Tamura Myōjin)
*: It is said that when Sakanoue no Tamuramaro deposited his bows and arrows ({{ill|Bow and arrow|ja|弓箭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bows and Arrows|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 弓矢|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q19827042}}), {{ill|Fun'ya no Watamaro|ja|文室綿麻呂|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fumimuro Watamaro|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q2713178}} built a hall at that spot. {{Refnest|group=注|『三國地誌』巻之二十三 伊勢國 鈴鹿郡 神祠}}
* The remains of the shrine festival site at Suzuka Pass
